spec.full_target:
A sphere-valued map cannot vanish outside a compact set. As approved by
the user on 2026-10-23, interpret spatial compact support as compact support
of a perturbation from a **fixed unit vector**, locally uniformly in time.
This is a disclosed nontrivial interpretation, not a claimed author-issued
correction.

Let \(n,m\geq1\) be integers and let
\(u:\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^m\) be jointly smooth.
Fix \(q\in\mathbb R^m\) with \(|q|=1\). Assume:

1. \(|u(x,t)|=1\) for all \(x\) and \(t>0\).
2. The acceleration \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu\) is normal to the sphere at
   \(u\): at each point there is a real scalar \(a(x,t)\) with
   \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu=a u\). No regularity of the selected scalar is
   assumed.
3. For every \(0<s<t<\infty\), a compact set
   \(C_{[s,t]}\subset\mathbb R^n\) exists such that \(u(x,r)=q\) for
   \(x\notin C_{[s,t]}\), \(r\in[s,t]\).

With Euclidean norms and Lebesgue measure, define

\[
e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|^2+\sum_{j=1}^n|\partial_{x_j}u(x,t)|^2,
\qquad E(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e(x,t)\,dx.
\]

The spatial gradient square is the Frobenius square, and
\(\Delta_xu=\sum_j\partial_{x_jx_j}u\) component by component.
Prove integrability of \(e(\cdot,t)\), differentiability of \(E\),
and \(E'(t)=0\) for every \(t>0\). No assertion at time zero is required.
spec.conclusion: For every real t>0, e(·,t) is Lebesgue integrable on ℝ^n, E is differentiable at t, and E'(t)=0. Moreover E(s)=E(t) for all real s,t>0. The energy is exactly ∫_{ℝ^n} (|u_t|²+Σ_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u|²) dx, without a factor 1/2; no conclusion at time zero is asserted.

definitions.definition: Ω=ℝ^n × (0,∞), the domain of u, with the relative Euclidean smooth structure.

definitions.type: partial differentiation notation on the open domain Ω
definitions.definition: ∂ denotes ordinary coordinate partial differentiation, component by component for vector-valued functions. Subscripts t and tt denote one and two time derivatives, x_j and x_jx_j denote one and two derivatives in spatial coordinate j, and x_jt denotes first time then spatial differentiation. Thus u_t=∂_t u, u_tt=∂_t∂_t u and ∂_{x_j}u_t=∂_{x_j}∂_t u. The same notation applies to real scalar functions such as e and g. Derivatives are used only where their existence has been established. For native total-function source applications, a function on Ω may be extended by zero outside Ω; at points of Ω all derivatives refer to its germ on Ω, independent of the extension.

definitions.type: spatial Laplacian on vector-valued twice differentiable functions on Ω

definitions.definition: e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|²+Σ_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u(x,t)|². All norms are Euclidean; the spatial sum is the Frobenius square of the spatial gradient.

E(t)=∫_{ℝ^n}e(x,t) dx for t>0. For definiteness this is the total real Bochner integral convention (zero if not integrable); the proof separately proves integrability for every t>0, so the intended ordinary finite Lebesgue integral is obtained.

definitions.type: Lebesgue measure and integration notation on finite real coordinate spaces
definitions.definition: dx is standard Lebesgue measure on ℝ^n, identified with the finite product of one-dimensional Lebesgue measures in standard coordinates. On other real coordinate spaces the same notation means their standard Lebesgue measure, including mass one on the zero-dimensional space. Integrable means measurable with finite integral of the absolute value. A set indicator 1_A is 1 on A and 0 elsewhere, for any set A in the integration space.
v·w=dot(v,w)=Σ_{k=1}^d v_k w_k for v,w∈ℝ^d and any finite dimension d; |v|²=v·v.

argument.text: Fix arbitrary x∈ℝ^n and t>0. H002 is smoothness on the open set Ω. Repeatedly apply M009 over ℝ to the zero extension of u on Ω with both smoothness orders ∞; since ∞+1=∞ this gives smoothness of its iterated derivatives on Ω. Evaluation of these continuous multilinear derivatives on fixed coordinate vectors gives the ordinary smooth partial derivatives. M002, over ℝ at (x,t), with order 2, then gives equality of time-space mixed second derivatives, by evaluating the symmetric second derivative on the time and j-th spatial coordinate vectors. Finite sums, scalar products and products of smooth real components are smooth, so e and e_t are continuous. M001 applied along the time line to u with itself gives ∂_t(u·u)=2u·u_t. H004 says u·u=1 throughout Ω; its derivative is zero. Thus u·u_t=0.

produces.statement: All partial derivatives of u are smooth on Ω, e and e_t are continuous on Ω, mixed second time-space derivatives agree, and u(x,t)·u_t(x,t)=0.

argument.text: Choose a from H005 at (x,t). By F001 and the finite-sum definition of the scalar product, u_t·(u_tt−Δ_xu)=u_t·(a u)=a(u_t·u)=0. This uses no derivative or regularity of the selected scalar. For completeness, M001 along time, applied to u and u_t, differentiates the identity u·u_t=0 and yields |u_t|²+u·u_tt=0. Applying the same product rule first to u·u=1 and then to u·∂_{x_j}u=0 along any spatial coordinate line gives u·∂_{x_jx_j}u=−|∂_{x_j}u|². Dotting the normality equation with u and using u·u=1 therefore gives a=Σ_j|∂_{x_j}u|²−|u_t|². Since this calculation uses only the defining equation for a, it holds for every scalar satisfying it.

produces.statement: At (x,t), u_t·(u_tt−Δ_xu)=0; every scalar satisfying u_tt−Δ_xu=a u equals Σ_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u|²−|u_t|².

argument.text: M001 applied along time to u_t with itself gives ∂_t|u_t|²=2u_t·u_tt. Applied to ∂_{x_j}u with itself, it gives ∂_t|∂_{x_j}u|²=2∂_{x_j}u·∂_t∂_{x_j}u; the mixed-derivative equality of F001 replaces the last factor by ∂_{x_j}u_t. Differentiating the finite spatial sum gives e_t=2u_t·u_tt+2Σ_j∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t. Together with F001 and F002 this proves every clause of the output for the arbitrary point. The witness a does not escape: the assertion about it is universal conditional on its displayed equation.

argument.text: Fix t0>0 and define J=[t0/2,3t0/2]. Its endpoints satisfy 0<t0/2<3t0/2, so H006 supplies a compact C with u=q outside C for all times in J. Apply M008 with real-valued function x↦|x| on C. The norm is continuous, so there is a real upper bound on these norms. Increasing it to a strictly positive number larger than it gives a real R>0 with |x_j|≤|x|<R for all x∈C and all j. Consequently a suitable R with C⊂(−R,R)^n exists, also when C is empty.

produces.statement: There exists a real R>0 such that C⊂(−R,R)^n.

argument.text: Choose R as in F001 and put Q=[−R,R]^n. In the coordinate order this is a closed order interval; M014 gives its compactness in finite real coordinate space. It is closed and therefore Lebesgue measurable. M013 with both endpoints constant −R,R gives |Q|=(2R)^n<∞. Here H001 provides positive finite dimensions. M011 for any real constant on Q, followed by M012 since Q is measurable, shows that every constant times 1_Q is integrable.

produces.statement: C⊂int Q, Q is compact and measurable, |Q|=(2R)^n<∞, and for every real b the function b 1_Q is integrable.

argument.text: On the open set (ℝ^n\C)×int J the map is the constant q: compact C is closed in Euclidean space, and H006 gives equality there. At every point of this open set all positive-order derivatives of u are zero, since locally the difference quotients of a constant are zero, and this applies repeatedly to its derivatives. N001 supplies smoothness of every derivative. Thus for every r∈int J, e,e_t,u_t·u_tt,u_t·Δ_xu and the listed derivative products vanish outside C. For g_j(x)=u_t(x,r)·∂_{x_j}u(x,r), smoothness follows by finite products and sums of the smooth components. Both g_j and its derivative are smooth and zero outside C as well. All scalar functions in the output are continuous. Their nonzero sets have closures contained in the closed compact C, hence their topological supports are compact.

produces.statement: On (ℝ^n\C)×int J all positive-order derivatives of u vanish. For every r∈int J, the scalar functions e(·,r), e_t(·,r), u_t·u_tt, u_t·Δ_xu, and for every spatial j the functions ∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t, u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u, g_j=u_t·∂_{x_j}u, and ∂_{x_j}g_j are continuous, vanish outside C, and have compact topological support contained in C; g_j is smooth.

argument.text: M007 applies to each of the continuous compactly supported scalar functions of F003 on ℝ^n, with Lebesgue measure finite on compact sets, and gives integrability. M008 on Q applied to the absolute value of each such function gives a finite bound, which may be enlarged to be nonnegative. Since the function is zero off Q, its absolute value is bounded everywhere by this constant times 1_Q. F002 and monotonicity of the integral give the absolute-integral estimate stated in the output. In particular t0∈int J, so e(·,t0) is integrable. The construction works for arbitrary t0>0 and proves the entire quantified assertion of the output. H002 ensures that every appearance of e is within its defining smoothness guard.

argument.text: Fix t0>0 and choose the matching C,R from N002. Set J=[t0/2,3t0/2], Q=[−R,R]^n and η=t0/4>0. Then [t0−η,t0+η]⊂int J. The box Q×[t0−η,t0+η] is compact by M014, viewed as a closed coordinate order interval in ℝ^n×ℝ, and lies in Ω. N001 gives continuity of e_t there. M008 applied to |e_t| on this box gives a finite upper bound. Enlarging it to be nonnegative proves the existence of a real B≥0 bounding |e_t| throughout this box.

produces.statement: There exists a real B≥0 such that |e_t(x,r)|≤B for all x∈Q and r∈[t0−η,t0+η]. Also [t0−η,t0+η]⊂int J.

argument.text: Choose B from F001, and define the family D_h as declared. For fixed x∈Q and 0<|h|<η, apply M004 to r↦e(x,r) on the closed interval between t0 and t0+h, with constant B. Both endpoints are interior times of J. The derivative exists by N001 and is bounded by F001; its within-interval derivative equals that ordinary derivative on the nondegenerate interval. Whether h is positive or negative, M004 gives |e(x,t0+h)−e(x,t0)|≤B|h|. Division by |h| gives |D_h(x)|≤B. For x∉Q, N002 gives zero density at both times, so |D_h(x)|≤B 1_Q(x) everywhere. N002 also states integrability of this majorant. Each D_h is continuous and measurable and is integrable by linearity from the two integrable density sections of N002.

produces.statement: For every real h with 0<|h|<η, D_h is continuous and integrable and |D_h(x)|≤B 1_Q(x) for all x∈ℝ^n. The majorant B 1_Q is integrable. For each x∈ℝ^n, D_h(x)→e_t(x,t0) as h→0 through nonzero real h.

argument.text: The pointwise limit in F002 is precisely the definition of the time derivative of e at (x,t0), supplied by N001. Apply M003 with spatial measure dx, real codomain, index h∈ℝ and filter of nonzero h tending to 0, F(h)=D_h and limit function x↦e_t(x,t0). This filter is countably generated: the punctured intervals 0<|h|<1/k for positive integers k form a countable neighborhood basis. F002 gives eventual strong measurability (continuous real functions), the bound, integrability of B1_Q and pointwise convergence. Therefore ∫D_h dx→∫e_t(x,t0)dx as h→0, h≠0.

produces.statement: As h→0 through nonzero real h, ∫_{ℝ^n}D_h(x)dx→∫_{ℝ^n}e_t(x,t0)dx.

argument.text: For all sufficiently small nonzero h, integrability from N002 and linearity show ∫D_h dx=(E(t0+h)−E(t0))/h. Both energies are the actual finite integrals, not merely total-integral defaults. F003 is thus the derivative limit for E at t0 and proves E'(t0)=∫e_t(x,t0)dx. Substituting the formula for e_t from N001, and using finite-sum and scalar linearity on the integrable terms from N002, gives E'(t0)=2∫u_t·u_tt dx+2Σ_j∫∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t dx. All these integrals are finite by N002. Since t0>0 was arbitrary, this proves the output.

argument.text: Fix t0>0 and spatial index j, and choose matching C,R from N002, putting Q=[−R,R]^n. H001 gives n≥1. Define g(x)=u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}u(x,t0). N001 gives smoothness of its factors; M001 on each j-coordinate line gives ∂_{x_j}g=∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u+u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u. N002 states that all three scalar terms are continuous, integrable, and zero outside C. Since C⊂int Q, the function g is identically zero near the boundary of Q. In particular its values on both faces x_j=±R are zero.

produces.statement: g is smooth, ∂_{x_j}g=∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u+u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u, and g, this derivative, and both summands are continuous, integrable, and zero outside C⊂int Q. On both faces x_j=±R, g=0.

argument.text: At fixed remaining coordinates, integrate ∂_{x_j}g first over x_j∈[−R,R]. The one-dimensional section of g is smooth; its derivative is continuous on this finite interval and hence interval integrable. M005 gives the integral as g at the upper endpoint minus g at the lower endpoint, zero by F001. To pass to the n-dimensional integral, M010 splits standard Lebesgue coordinates into the j-th coordinate and the remaining n−1 coordinates; its inverse is coordinate insertion. Thus the product measure is exactly dx, not an unspecified proportional measure. Apply M006 to ∂_{x_j}g times the indicator of Q in these coordinates. It is integrable, because by F001 the indicator does not change the function. Both product measures (Lebesgue on [−R,R] or on the full coordinate factors with the box indicator) are sigma-finite and hence s-finite. Integrating the remaining coordinates gives ∫_Q∂_{x_j}g dx=0. When n=1 the remaining space has dimension zero and measure one; the same assertion is precisely the preceding one-dimensional FTC.

All terms in F001 vanish off Q, so F002 and linearity imply 0=∫_{ℝ^n}∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u dx+∫_{ℝ^n}u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u dx. Symmetry of the real scalar product and rearrangement give the asserted integration-by-parts formula, including finiteness from F001. Universal introduction over t0 and j proves the entire output.

argument.text: For every t>0, N002 gives integrability of e(·,t). N003 proves differentiability of E there and its derivative formula. For each such t substitute N004 into that formula and use linearity for the finite integrable sum, obtaining E'(t)=2∫u_t·u_tt dx−2Σ_j∫u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u dx=2∫u_t·(u_tt−Δ_xu) dx. N001 makes the last integrand identically zero. Thus E'(t)=0 for every t>0. H002 supplies the smoothness guard on the definitions of e and E.

argument.text: For arbitrary positive real endpoints s<t, F001 gives differentiability throughout [s,t] and zero derivative there. M004 with real function E and C=0 gives |E(t)−E(s)|≤0, and therefore equality. If the endpoints coincide equality is immediate, and if their order is reversed exchange them. This proves E(s)=E(t) for all s,t>0. In invoking the native total-function M004, extend E by zero at nonpositive times; [s,t] is inside its positive domain so this does not affect any derivative. The defining energy retains coefficient 1 on both squares and there is no assertion at time zero. Together with F001 this is exactly P.
